title: 7 Things AI-Native Companies Do Differently
dek: On this Long Read Sunday, NLW pulls together what Stripe, Shopify, Uber, Ramp, Cloudflare and a wave of AI-native startups have published about running agents in production. Seven shared practices emerge, and most come back to context. The idea that didn't make the list: agents as teammates.

oneIdea.headline: AI-native companies don't hire agent teammates. They turn the company into a system.
oneIdea.summary: The most aggressive adopters share seven practices. They give agents the whole picture, put agents in every function, let signals rather than prompts start the work, run orchestrators that spin up sub-agents, make agents check each other and show proof, scale human review to risk while keeping a person accountable, and run one shared system that improves itself. What's missing is the fixed roster of named, persistent agent coworkers many expected. In practice, work looks less like managing teammates and more like engaging an on-demand consulting firm: you bring a goal, a lead staffs it, evidence comes back, and you own the result. The durable asset is context, not the agents.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: A scribe is a tool, not a colleague
items.body: The most useful finding here for general practice is a small study in the Harvard Business Review: managers checked identical documents less carefully when they were labelled as coming from an AI teammate, with scrutiny about 16 per cent lower at firms that already treat AI as staff. NLW notes it is one early study. It fits what we know of automation bias. An AI scribe's note should be read as a draft from a tool, and the clinician who signs it owns it.

items.title: Review scaled to risk, with a named owner
items.body: The companies described match human checking to risk and keep one person accountable through every handoff. That is ordinary clinical governance. A scribe's summary of a routine consultation needs a read-through; a generated referral, a medication change or anything going to a coroner needs proper checking. If a practice adopts tools that act on incoming results or letters without a prompt, decide beforehand who is responsible for each stream.

items.title: Stale context, and who pays for the tokens
items.body: Ramp found its agent got worse when the information it relied on went out of date. The same applies to practice protocols, templates and formularies fed into any tool: someone has to maintain them. On cost the two sides differ. NLW describes agents checking agents at great volume; Zitron says that volume costs more to serve than it is priced at. A supplier adding agentic features may move to usage-based charging, so fix prices in the contract.

the_other_side.text: Zitron has not written about these seven practices. His nearest piece, published twelve days before this edition, argues that the heavy agent use Whittemore admires was an anomaly he calls token-maxxing: companies let staff spend freely, then pulled back when costs soared, and he cites Uber burning its annual token budget in a single quarter. He says agents add a layer of cost, since each needs its own virtual machine and may run several models at once, and judges that even good results are mediocre. He points to Replit, whose margin reportedly turned negative after it launched a more autonomous agent. These are his claims and opinions.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is the cost of a unit of verified work when agents do it at unsubsidised prices. Both accept as fact that the heaviest adopters run agents in great volume, that Uber is among them, and that checking the output has become the constraint. The empirical question is whether these fleets pay for themselves once prices reflect their cost; the observable is whether the companies Whittemore cites keep expanding agent use after budgets are capped, and whether measures such as Shopify's revert rate are published. The residue is worldview: whether a company rebuilt around agents is a new kind of organisation or an expensive habit. For Whittemore to be vindicated, the seven practices must spread beyond engineering and survive price rises. For Zitron, usage must fall back as subsidies end and venture-funded customers retrench. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both treat verification and cost, not model ability, as the limit. Watch whether Uber and Ramp report agent volumes again next quarter.

headlines.headline: Agents as teammates is the wrong mental model
headlines.summary: NLW once ran a full team of OpenClaws: researchers, writers, project coordinators and a chief of staff above them. He's increasingly convinced that framing doesn't reflect how the most sophisticated users actually work with agents.

headlines.headline: Watch what engineers do today to see your next six months
headlines.summary: Code got there first because it has tests, verifiability and a clear definition of done, so not every practice will transfer cleanly. Still, NLW argues that watching engineers today is the best preview of what everyone else will be doing in three to six months.

headlines.headline: Practice 1: give agents everything an employee can see
headlines.summary: The limit on serious knowledge work isn't the model; it's the context the model can reach. Francis Davidson, whose under-a-year-old company OpenAI acquired, calls his approach "content maxing": agents get MCP or CLI access to every meeting recording, Slack, email, Drive and every company tool.

headlines.headline: A stealable idea: a clean shared document for every decision
headlines.summary: Davidson's team also writes a shared document for every decision, and agents keep that knowledge base current. The result is a track record of what was decided, what went into it and how the call was made.

headlines.headline: The context layer has to be maintained like a product
headlines.summary: Ramp pipes Slack, Notion, Linear and Calendar into persistent memory every day so agent sessions never start cold. Uber built a context graph across 30+ internal systems, and Shopify's monorepo holds skills, runbooks and instruction files written for agents. The catch: Ramp found its analyst agent gets worse when that layer goes stale.

headlines.headline: Employees are hoarding context as job security
headlines.summary: One founder found that rich context has a political side: employees unsure about their future are holding back knowledge, because handing it to the agent feels like handing over their value. NLW calls it a cultural problem far more than a technical one, and one leaders will have to face head-on.

headlines.headline: Practice 2: agents in every function, not just engineering
headlines.summary: Anthropic's growth marketing team has at times been one person, using agents to flag underperforming ads and sub-agents to write hundreds of new ones in minutes. OpenAI's Enterprise Signals research found Basis running customer onboarding with agents and Clay giving every account its own workspace and sub-agent.

headlines.headline: Practice 3: a signal, not a prompt, starts the work
headlines.summary: In AI-native companies, work kicks off from triggers such as a customer message, an invoice, a renewal or an operational alert, with no human translating it into a prompt. At Uber, most agent sessions are now started by other agents, for code review, self-healing CI and on-call triage.

headlines.headline: Stop asking what to ask the AI. Ask what should start work on its own.
headlines.summary: Outside engineering, the exercise is to list the business events that should trigger work automatically: a churn signal, a renewal coming due, an invoice arriving.

headlines.headline: Practice 4: one orchestrator, many disposable sub-agents
headlines.summary: Anthropic's research system has a lead agent plan the work and spin up parallel sub-agents, each with its own task, context and output format, and none aware of the others. It scales from one agent for a fact check to 10+ for hard problems, and it beat a single agent by about 90% on internal research evals.

headlines.headline: The orchestrator routes. It doesn't do the work.
headlines.summary: Warp's orchestrator only decides which agents, which models and which slice of context each job gets. The logic comes back to context windows: the orchestrator holds the summaries, and each worker gets a narrow instruction and a clean slate.

headlines.headline: Practice 5: verification is now the bottleneck, so build for it
headlines.summary: Across knowledge work, the constraint has moved from producing work to verifying it. AI-native organizations treat checking as its own job with dedicated systems, and an agent's work isn't done just because it produced something.

headlines.headline: Shopify treats every security finding as a claim that must be proven
headlines.summary: If the agent can't write a test that actually exploits the bug, the finding is rejected or downgraded, and a different model does the checking. At RunLayer, a fixing agent ships before-and-after evidence, a second agent reviews it adversarially, and a QA agent tries to break it in production.

headlines.headline: Practice 6: scale human review to risk, and always know who owns it
headlines.summary: Uber carries a chain of responsibility through every agent-to-agent call, so even long handoffs trace back to a specific person. Stripe's agents write the code but humans merge every change, while RunLayer lets small, low-risk changes merge on their own.

headlines.headline: Snap puts more than half its agent spend into guardrails
headlines.summary: Ramp is selling the same risk-tiering idea for finance: agents that approve low-risk expenses on their own or recommend a decision with their reasoning, with each customer setting where the agents have to stop.

headlines.headline: Practice 7: one shared system instead of everyone doing AI their own way
headlines.summary: Ramp keeps 350 shared workflows in one library, with a tool that recommends skills based on your role. Uber's library holds 3,600 skills that run more than 30,000 times a day.

headlines.headline: Shopify's coding agent only works in public Slack channels
headlines.summary: There are no DMs, so every agent session becomes a transcript anyone can search and learn from.

headlines.headline: Agents that grade the agents and propose fixes
headlines.summary: At Warp, scoring agents grade finished runs, and another agent proposes system improvements as pull requests for the team to review. The caution is to measure the right thing: Shopify doesn't count lines of AI code or PRs, and tracks how often changes get reverted instead.

headlines.headline: The teammate metaphor was a useful bridge, not the destination
headlines.summary: What it got right was moving people from AI as a chat window to AI that goes out and does work on its own. It helped the transition from assisted AI to agentic AI, even if it isn't how the most advanced users ended up working.

headlines.headline: Fleets that scale with the job beat fixed rosters
headlines.summary: Instead of a fixed roster, capacity follows the job: fresh context for every task, swappable models, and company-wide knowledge in place of personal memory. Anthropic's guidance found that splitting agents by role, such as planner, coder, tester and reviewer, tends to backfire, because each handoff becomes a game of telephone.

headlines.headline: A bitter lesson for org design: stop organizing agents like people
headlines.summary: It's natural to manage agents the way we manage humans, but in one experiment, role-split agents spent more effort coordinating than working. Every tried a proxy agent for each person early in the year and moved to a few agents at the intersections that expand through sub-agents as needed.

headlines.headline: Keep the context persistent, not the agent
headlines.summary: NLW's own setup has flipped. Instead of named OpenClaw agents with a chief of staff, his Claude Code and Codex projects are organized around shared context in repositories, and agents get spun up for specific tasks. There's no anthropomorphized agent, just a persistent bundle of context he can drop any agents into.

headlines.headline: The better analogy: on-demand consulting firms
headlines.summary: You bring a goal, an engagement lead staffs it, and you never manage or even meet the staff. The deliverable comes back with evidence and you own the result. When the engagement ends the workers are gone, but the work and its records stay, and the methodology can improve each time.

headlines.headline: Labeling AI as a teammate made managers check its work less carefully
headlines.summary: In an HBR-published study with BCG, managers reviewed identical error-planted documents labeled as from an AI tool, a colleague named Alex, or an AI teammate named "Alex 3," and scrutinized the AI teammate's work less. At companies that already treat AI as employees, scrutiny dropped about 16%. NLW cautions it's one early study.

headlines.headline: Named personal agents are really orchestrators in disguise
headlines.summary: Consumer products that have you name a personal agent don't contradict the shift. They're the ur-orchestrators: holding all the context about your life, dispatching whatever agents are needed, and leaving you a single point of contact.
